column4: The verse stages the section's whole weather sequence: winds announce mercy, bear heavy cloud, carry it to dead land, and rain brings fruit and the dead forth. It makes the growing Lord visible through rain's work on earth.
The driven, joined, piled cloud yields rain from within it. Its layered mass directly meets the source's dictionary image of cloud upon cloud (rabābah) before water descends.
Allah sends winds that raise cloud, spreads it through the sky and makes it fragments before rain falls. This supplies the cloud-and-wind movement behind the section's growing cloud.
Winds raise cloud, then it is driven to dead land and gives that land life. The verse joins the cloud scene to the section's claim that water restores and sustains earth.
After despair, He sends غَيْث and spreads mercy, ending as al-Ḥamīd. Rain, mercy, and the H-M-D word named for 1:2 stand together as the section says they do.
The reader is told to look at the آثار, or effects, of divine mercy: it revives earth after death. This gives a Qur'anic counterpart to the first rain's green trace written on soil.
If people remain upright on the way (استقاموا), God gives abundant water. It is the unusually explicit union of the Q-W-M/straightness family behind mustaqīm with water that holds life up.

At the start of the Midian sequence, Moses asks his Lord to guide him to the right road; 28:23 then brings him to water. This ayah contributes the guided traveller, which the next ayah locates at the well.
Moses reaches the water of Midian and finds people watering, while two women hold back their flocks. It is the Qur'an's concrete wellhead scene of water, herd, and those unable to draw.
Moses waters for the two women, turns to shade, and addresses “Rabbi” as needy of any good sent down. Watering, shade, need, and the R-B-B word converge exactly as in the source's well image.

Joseph's brothers propose putting him in the dark recess of a well so travellers may pick him up. It gives the well its opposite depth: water's mouth and bucket can also conceal a vulnerable traveller.
A caravan's water-drawer lowers his bucket (دلو), then discovers Joseph. The act of drawing water makes the buried child appear, a direct counterpart to the section's pulley-and-well mouth.

The question imagines water becoming غَوْرًا, sunk beyond reach, and asks who could bring flowing water. It is the direct boundary to the full well and accessible water on which a traveller's affairs stand.
Water is sent from the sky in a measured amount and settled within the earth, while God can remove it. It joins measured rain to hidden ground-water, the two routes of water in the section.

God sends water from heaven and conducts it as springs within the earth, then brings varied crops whose later drying is visible. It directly connects rain, subterranean water, cultivation, and the changing green surface.
Moses names the Lord of the worlds (Rabb al-ʿālamīn); 26:78–79 immediately specify guidance, food, and drink. The title named in 1:2 frames the source's linked guidance-and-water claims.
“Who created me, then guides me” stands immediately before the declaration that He feeds and waters Moses. It gives the section's path and its water the same divine speaker and sequence.
The same Lord says, in Moses's first-person confession, that He feeds and waters him. It is the section's traveller-water thesis stated as dependence on God.
Moses says their Lord gives each thing its form and then guides it; 20:53 follows with paths, rain, and plants. Its own contribution is the measured, guiding Lord behind the material scene.
God makes paths on earth, sends down sky-water, and brings out pairs of plants. This is a compact Qur'anic meeting of road, rain, and growing vegetation.
The plants are food for people and their anʿām. The N-ʿ-M root named for 1:7 appears in the livestock that the preceding rain-and-path scene sustains.
The command to look at human food introduces the water-and-soil sequence in 80:25–32. It turns the source's agricultural image into a deliberate act of seeing.
“We poured down water in abundance” begins the food sequence. This is rain as the generous descent that makes the source's cloud and soil productive.
The earth is then split open. Its own action supplies the cracked soil through which the poured water becomes visible growth.
Grain is caused to grow from the opened earth. It is a precise outcome of the rain-and-soil sequence rather than a generic provision claim.
Grapes and fodder appear in the same sequence. The fodder continues the section's concern for water that feeds both people and grazing creatures.
Olives and palms are listed as products of the irrigated earth. They extend the source's growing vegetation from tender herb to lasting food plants.
Dense gardens are one result of the poured water and split earth. Their gathered growth parallels the source's emphasis on water collected and vegetation made abundant.
Fruit and pasture complete the plant scene. Pasture directly meets the soft, living ground-cover developed in the source.
The entire sequence is provision for people and their anʿām. It joins the named N-ʿ-M family to water-fed livelihood for human and animal alike.
Water is driven to barren land, producing crop eaten by people and their anʿām. The verse makes water's movement into dry ground and its sustaining result explicit.
The earth is spread out; 79:31 specifies that its water and pasture are brought forth. This ayah gives the prepared ground whose next ayah unites underground water with grazing.
God brings from the earth its water and its pasture. It directly pairs the well-side source of water with the green surface it supports.

The signs include sky-water reviving dead earth, creatures dispersed through it, changing winds, and cloud held between sky and earth. It gathers the section's rain, wind, cloud, life, and ordered world in one ayah.
Water comes down from al-samāʾ and brings out vegetation, green growth, grain, palms, vines, olives, and pomegranates. It realizes the source's S-M-W dictionary meeting of sky, rain, and plant.
Sky-water is both drink and the growth in which herds are pastured. It gives the rain a double use central to the section: a traveller's water and animal-sustaining green land.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit. It spells out the growth attributed in the source to the cloud called by the R-B-B family.
God sends water from the sky and gives life to earth after its death. It is the rain-to-revival relation without an intervening metaphor.
When water reaches the lifeless earth, it stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful pair. The bodily verbs give detailed form to the source's earth marked and enlivened by rain.
Rain from heaven makes the earth green. The verse offers the immediate visual result of the first rain's plant-mark in the source.
Winds arrive as good news before mercy and pure water is sent down from the sky. This directly joins beneficent wind, mercy, and potable rain.
The pure water gives life to dead land and gives drink to many cattle and people. It makes explicit the shared human-and-animal livelihood implied by the source's well and pasture.
Water from heaven grows gardens of delight whose trees humans cannot make grow. The verse sharpens the section's claim that the cloud's nurture belongs to the Lord, not the soil alone.
Asked who sends sky-water and revives earth after death, people answer Allah. It closely states the source's rain, life, and Lord relation as a confession.
Water from heaven makes every noble kind of plant grow. Its emphasis on diverse paired growth extends the source's tender grass and cultivated earth.
The earth is humble and lifeless, then water makes it stir and swell. This repeats the source's life-bearing rain in a sign that points beyond the visible ground.
Water descends from the sky in due measure and revives a dead land. Its “measure” joins the source's water that keeps an affair standing with the restraint under which rain is given.
Sky-water revives earth after death, while creatures and winds are distributed as signs. It keeps rain, living beings, and winds in the one ordered scene.
Blessed water descends from the sky and produces gardens and harvest grain. It is an especially direct form of the source's blessing-bearing cloud.
Tall palms bear clustered fruit as provision for servants. This gives a concrete, gathered abundance to the source's image of plentiful water and growth.
The blessed water gives life to dead land, and the verse compares this to coming forth after death. It preserves the source's earthly image while opening its resurrection horizon.
Noah promises that, if they turn back, God will send the sky upon them with abundant rain. Rain is presented as restorative generosity, not merely weather.
The rain promise unfolds as wealth, children, gardens, and rivers. It makes the source's water into the material support of a settled, flourishing life.
From the rain-bearing clouds comes abundant pouring water. The ayah directly supplies the water-laden cloud behind the section's layered sky.
The abundant water brings grain and vegetation. Its concise cause-and-result matches the section's cloud named for making plants grow.
Clusters of gardens follow the rain and vegetation. This is the gathered, fertile outcome of the preceding weather scene.
The command is to glorify the name of the highest Rabb; 87:2–5 then narrate proportion, guidance, pasture, and its dark remainder. It supplies the source's Lord-name at the head of that land image.
The Creator proportioned what He made, before 87:3 says He measured and guided and 87:4 brings pasture. The source's water-maintained order is illuminated by this ordered making.
“He measured and guided” stands immediately before the bringing-out of pasture. It joins the source's straightness/Q-W-M concern to a guided natural growth sequence.
He brings forth pasture. The ayah is the direct Qur'anic counterpart to the source's living tender herb.

The believers' visible sīmā, a W-S-M marking word named in the source, is followed in the same ayah by the likeness of a seed that shoots, strengthens, and stands on its stem. Mark, growth, and standing are fused here.
God makes the sky a canopy and sends water down from it to produce fruits as provision. The S-M-W word of the source is joined to rain and edible earth.
Moses asks for water for his people; twelve springs burst from the rock, and every group knows its drinking place. It makes water a shared order that keeps a community supplied.
Moses's people receive twelve springs, each tribe knowing its drinking place. The second telling confirms the source's concern with water as an ordered support rather than an undirected abundance.

Water descends from the sky, valleys flow by their capacity, and the flood carries foam while what benefits people remains. It supplies a bounded, gathered-water scene and distinguishes enduring benefit from surface overflow.
The spread earth is given mountains and made to grow everything in due balance. It gives the soil side of the source's measured, fit-for-life growth before rain appears in 15:22.
Fertilizing winds are sent and water comes down from the sky, which humans do not control as storekeepers. Wind, cloud-rain, and dependence meet the source's sustained wet wind and water.
Every living thing is made from water. This gives the source's practical water that holds life up its widest Qur'anic claim.
A dead land is given life and yields grain from which people eat. It is the same return from dead soil to sustenance that the rain passages make visible.
Gardens of palms and vines are made in that land, with springs flowing in them. It joins the source's well-water to cultivated plant abundance.
People eat the gardens' fruit, and the ayah asks whether they will give thanks. It connects rain-grown food to the praise/gratitude side of the source's ḥamd image.
God sends sky-water to bring out fruits as provision, and also subjects rivers and ships. It joins rain-grown food to water that carries travellers and sustains their affairs.

Hūd promises that turning back will bring abundant rain from the sky and added strength. The verse states rain as repair and strengthening, like the source's gloss on rain improving a people's condition.
Joseph foretells a year in which people receive rain and press produce. Rain returns after scarcity as agricultural recovery, a concrete communal version of the source's provision.
People are asked to consider the water they drink. The direct address makes everyday drink the object of the same attentive reading the source asks of rain and wells.
Did people send the drinking water down from the rain clouds, or did God? The ayah directly locates potable water in cloud and divine giving.
God places lofty mountains and gives sweet water to drink. The source's dictionary gloss for rabāb as plentiful, sweet water finds a Qur'anic scene of drinkable water provided from the land.

A garden on high ground yields double produce when struck by a heavy rain; even dew suffices. It closely parallels the source's soft plant that continues through summer and the productive effect of moisture.
Water is apportioned between the people and the she-camel, each drinking turn known. It makes water a regulated support shared across a human-and-animal community.
Moses is commanded to make a dry path through the sea for the people. The verse turns water from a source of thirst into a boundary through which guided travellers are preserved.
Rivers and paths are placed in the earth so that people may be guided. It makes the source's coupling of water and road a feature of the land itself.
At a moment of isolation and need, a stream is placed beneath Mary by her Lord. It is a focused scene of life-sustaining water arriving with divine care.
Good land brings out vegetation by its Lord's permission, while bad land yields only scant growth. It gives the fertile earth of the source its explicit contrary soil.
Sky-water mingles with earth's vegetation until it is adorned, then divine command leaves it harvested. It qualifies the source's fresh green growth with its sudden perishability.
Worldly life is likened to rain whose vegetation mingles with earth and then becomes dry fragments. The verse reverses the source's enduring tender herb into an image of passing growth.
Rain produces crop that delights growers, then it withers, yellows, and becomes debris. The full green-to-dry cycle throws the source's summer-unsinged herb into relief.
After bringing pasture out in 87:4, God makes it dark stubble. The ayah is the immediate reversal of the tender, living pasture developed in the source.
A garden with palms, vines, and rivers is struck by a fiery whirlwind and destroyed when its owner is vulnerable. It is a direct contrary fate for water-supported cultivated abundance.
A freezing wind strikes and destroys a people's cultivated field. The destructive wind is the contrary of the source's wet, growth-bearing south wind.
A people see a cloud and expect rain, but it is a painful wind. The verse sharply reverses the anticipated merciful cloud-and-rain scene.
The wind sent against ʿĀd is barren. It supplies the opposite of the source's moist, plant-growing wind.
God could make drinking water salty, then asks why people do not give thanks. It sets the loss of sweet water against the source's plentiful, drinkable support.
At the Flood's end, the earth is commanded to swallow its water and the sky to withhold. This boundary scene reverses the normal descent and retained abundance of rain and wells.

The source explicitly likens first-rain vegetation to a branded mark; this W-S-M verb threatens a brand on the snout. It preserves the marking sense while reversing green, life-bearing inscription into punishment.
Mary is told to shake the palm so fresh ripe dates fall; with 19:24's stream, the neighbouring ayah completes a water-and-plant provision scene for a needy person.
God makes the earth a resting place and places paths in it; 43:11 then gives measured sky-water. The ayah supplies the road that the following water enables.
Winds bring good news and a taste of mercy, while ships move by God's command so people seek bounty. It connects beneficent wind with travel over water and provision.
The verse shows lightning in fear and hope and raises heavy clouds. Its cloud is the charged, weighty counterpart to the source's layered rain cloud.
Many earlier peoples received abundant sky-rain, gardens, and rivers, yet perished. It retains the source's fertile water scene while showing that fertility alone does not secure a people.
Rain purifies the believers and makes their feet firm. Water here supports bodily steadiness on a threatened path, a specific analogue to the source's water that lets a journey continue.
After the watering and shade of 28:24, the woman comes to invite Moses to payment from her father. Its own contribution is the well scene's movement from needy traveller to livelihood and safety.
The cattle have benefits and drinks, followed by a call to give thanks; 36:33–35 has just shown the revived land, gardens, and springs. It extends that water-grown provision to animal life.

Wealth is called qiyāman, a means by which people are maintained. This closely matches the source's dictionary explanation of qiwām as what makes one stand and provides sufficient livelihood, even though the verse does not name water.
The two waters are set apart: one sweet and fresh, one salty and bitter. It clarifies the source's “sweet water” sense by marking the usable water against its opposite.
The fresh, sweet sea is contrasted with the salty, bitter one, while ships move through both. It adds travel to the contrast between water that can be drunk and water that cannot.
The gates of heaven open with pouring water. It is the overwhelming reversal of the source's life-giving rain: the same descent begins the Flood.
Springs burst from earth and waters meet for a decreed matter. It reverses the well's sustaining hidden water into earth-water joined with sky-water to overwhelm.
Both gardens produce their fruit and a river runs between them. The cultivated, watered garden gives a settled counterpart to the source's rain-made vegetation.
The garden's water may become sunk in the ground so its owner cannot seek it. This is a precise negative image of the accessible well and the flowing water of 67:30.
Job is directed to strike the ground, where water is cool for washing and drinking. The scene gives ground-water a healing, sustaining use alongside the source's well.
The she-camel and the people each have a known turn at the water. It develops the source's well as a social resource whose life-giving use is apportioned.
Talut's travelling force is tested at a river: only a small handful may be drunk. Water remains necessary for a journey, but its withholding tests whether the travellers can keep to command.
The deniers demand that a spring gush from the earth. This makes a ground-water source an object of skeptical demand, in contrast to the given rain and well scenes of the source.
The source's W-S-M dictionary sense is a visible mark left by the first rain; this ayah says the poor can be recognised by their sīmā. The link is limited to that marking sense, not a water scene.
The people of the heights recognise each group by their sīmā. It offers the same W-S-M notion of a legible identifying mark that the source applies, figuratively, to rain-written vegetation.
The people of the heights recognise men by their sīmā before addressing them. As with 7:46, the connection is only the source's secondary mark/branding sense, so it remains weak.
Sinners are recognised by their sīmā. It repeats the named W-S-M marking vocabulary, but supplies no rain or soil scene; its relevance is confined to the source's “mark” layer.
